messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Margaret Chen was forty-two when a delivery truck ran a red light and struck the passenger side of her sedan. She had been driving home from a community outreach event—the kind of work she had done for fifteen years as a social ministry worker, coordinating support services for low-income families in the city's northeast parishes. The impact came without warning. One moment she was turning onto Maple Street; the next, the truck's grille filled her peripheral vision and the world became noise and metal and the sensation of her body no longer being her own. She was conscious through all of it: conscious of the car folding around her, conscious of her arm pinned against the door frame, conscious of not being able to move or stop what was happening to her. The police report noted that the truck driver had not even attempted to brake. The report also noted that Margaret had been driving at the posted speed limit, in her lane, with the light in her favor. Nothing she had done caused the crash. Nothing she could have done would have prevented it. Yet when she learned that the driver had received only a citation for running the red light—no criminal charges, no meaningful consequence—something inside her calcified. The citation was later dismissed on a technicality. The driver's insurance company settled with hers, a transaction that felt to Margaret like the conversion of her trauma into a check amount. No apology was ever offered. No accountability was ever established. The unfairness of it—that she had done everything right and suffered everything, while the person responsible had faced nothing—became a second injury layered over the first.

In the months that followed, Margaret came to understand her body as fundamentally unreliable—not because of her injuries, which were significant but ultimately healed, but because it had betrayed her by being in that car at that moment, moving in that direction, vulnerable to forces entirely beyond her control. She had come to believe that her own body could not be trusted to keep her safe, that something essential inside her had broken on impact and never fully mended. The injustice of it gnawed at her constantly. She would lie awake at night thinking about the truck driver going about his life, unchanged, unaccountable, while she remained imprisoned by what he had done. She had come to believe that the world operated on a principle of radical unfairness, that doing everything right offered no protection, and that nothing—not law, not justice, not the basic moral order she had spent her career trying to uphold—could be relied upon.

For the first three weeks after discharge, Margaret tried to return to work. She had been scheduled to lead a workshop on accessing mental health resources. She sat in her office—a small converted storage room in the basement of St. Catherine's Church—and found that her hands shook when she tried to type. More troubling was the way her mind now worked: she could not relax, could not let her guard down, because relaxation felt like surrender, like an invitation for something terrible to happen. When she tried to sit quietly for even a few minutes, her chest would tighten and her breathing would shallow. It was as though her body was telling her that safety required constant vigilance, that any moment of peace was a moment when disaster could strike. So she stopped trying to rest. She filled her evenings with tasks—organizing files, preparing materials, anything to remain in motion, in control.

The avoidance came gradually. Within two months, Margaret had stopped driving altogether. She told herself it was temporary, a reasonable precaution while she adjusted. But as weeks became months, the thought of being in a vehicle—whether driving or as a passenger—generated such acute dread that she simply could not do it. Her colleagues began to notice that she was no longer attending off-site meetings. When they offered rides, she declined with vague excuses. The truth was that the image of cars hitting other cars had become intrusive and unbidden; she would see it when she closed her eyes, see it in the moment before she fell asleep. The idea of placing herself in a vehicle felt like volunteering for re-traumatization. Her work began to suffer. The social ministry position required occasional travel to partner agencies across the city. By the nine-month mark, Margaret's supervisor had gently suggested that her reduced availability was affecting her ability to fulfill her role. Rather than explain the true source of her limitations—which felt shameful, inexplicable, as though she were being held hostage by her own mind—Margaret requested a reduction to part-time hours. She worked from the office now, coordinating by phone and email, her world contracting to the rooms she could reach on foot.

The hypervigilance had become a constant companion. She scanned for exits the moment she entered any space, even familiar ones. She startled at ordinary sounds—a door slamming, a car backfiring in the street outside, the unexpected ring of a telephone—her body launching into fight-or-flight before her conscious mind could catch up. What frightened her most was the feeling that she could not trust her own judgment about safety. Even when colleagues or her therapist from the initial crisis counseling told her that she was safe, that the risk of another accident was statistically low, she could not believe them. Her body held a different truth: that the world was dangerous, that she was vulnerable, and that nothing—not statistics, not careful driving, not the reassurances of others, not even basic justice—could change that fundamental reality. Now, at forty-eight, Margaret has been living with these constraints for six years. She has not driven since the accident. She has not been a passenger in a car in almost as long. She still works part-time, still helps people, but increasingly from behind a desk. She has not dated in years; the thought of being dependent on someone else for transportation, or of explaining why she cannot go anywhere, feels impossible. What brought her finally to seek help was a moment three weeks ago when she realized she could not remember the last time she had felt safe—truly safe, not just the absence of immediate danger, but a sense that her body and her world were trustworthy. She sat in her apartment on a Tuesday evening and understood that she was no longer living a life; she was managing a disaster that had already passed. She is hoping that someone can help her understand why her mind will not let her move forward, why the unfairness of that single moment—the unfairness that was never answered, never resolved, never made right—continues to hold her captive, and whether it is possible to ever trust her own body or the world again.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress: Avoid Physical Stress is reported as a maladaptive strategy but does not appear in the vignette. While Margaret avoids driving and relaxation, there is no description of her avoiding situations that place physical stress on her body.
- Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people: Startle to Sounds is reported but only partially illustrated. The vignette mentions Margaret startling at 'a door slamming, a car backfiring in the street outside, the unexpected ring of a telephone,' which directly illustrates this symptom. Upon re-examination, this IS present in the vignette and should not have been flagged.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.
